title: The train search [[comes first]].
hook: A redesign concept for the IRCTC rail-booking homepage. I set the brief myself: make searching for a train the first thing the page asks of you.

facts.label: Role
facts.value: Page structure, hierarchy and visual design

facts.label: Why
facts.value: A brief I set myself. Not commissioned by IRCTC and not connected to it

facts.label: Platform
facts.value: Desktop web. One homepage, drawn 1,920 px wide

facts.label: Scope
facts.value: Homepage only. No results, payment or ticket screens

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Visual concept. Not built and not tested with users

summary: The problem I set myself: a rail-booking homepage has to offer dozens of services, yet it should be obvious where to search for a train.
What I did: I designed one long homepage in six bands. The train search fills the first screen and everything else sits below it.
The key idea: rank tasks by position. Booking comes first, checking a trip you already have sits on its edge, and other services and holidays follow.
Where it stands: a single desktop mock-up. It was not commissioned, built or tested, and it stops at the Search button.

lead.alt: The whole IRCTC homepage concept shown in three columns: the top with the train search and services, the middle with five holiday cards, and the end with the social strip and footer
lead.caption: The whole page, cut into three columns so it fits. Read it left to right: the search and services, then the holiday cards, then the footer.

sections.label: The brief
sections.heading: Nobody asked for this, so I wrote the brief

blocks.p: I chose this page as practice because it is a hard ordering problem. One homepage has to carry train booking, trip status, flights, hotels, buses, catering, holidays and a long list of rules and help pages.
My rule was simple. Someone who arrives knowing their route and date should be able to start a search without reading anything else. Everything else stays on the page, further down.

figures.alt: First screen of the concept with the header, a booking card on the left and a train photograph with the words Welcome to Indian Railways on the right
figures.caption: The first screen. The booking card takes the left half. The photograph and the welcome line take the right, so nothing else asks for a click.

aside.title: What this is not.
aside.detail: There was no client and no research. I did not study how people use the real site, so I make no claim that this version is faster or better. The emblems, logos, photographs and holiday text in the mock-up are placeholder content and belong to their owners.

sections.label: Structure
sections.heading: One long page in six bands

blocks.p: The design is a single page, 1,920 px wide and 5,400 px long. I split it into six bands. The header and the search together are 1,080 px tall, the height of a full HD screen.

figures.alt: Map of the page as six numbered bands with their heights: header, hero and train search, other services, curated holidays, social strip and footer
figures.caption: The six bands and how much of the page each one takes. Look at band 4: the holiday cards are 41% of the page length, more than twice the search.

blocks.p: That is the trade-off in this layout. The search is first, but most of the scrolling is promotion. Moving the holidays lower fixes the order. It does not make the page any shorter.
I sorted what the page offers into five kinds of task and gave each one a place. The more common I judged a task to be, the higher it sits. That was my own judgement. I had no usage data.

figures.alt: Diagram ranking five tasks by where they sit on the page: book a train, check an existing trip, use another travel service, browse holiday ideas, and look up everything else
figures.caption: The five tasks in order. The dashed line is the bottom of the first screen. Only booking and checking an existing trip sit above it.

blocks.p: Type size does not follow the same order, and that is a weakness. The two section headings further down are 60 px, larger than Book Tickets at 40 px. The card wins on position and colour, and loses on size.

sections.label: The search card
sections.heading: Five fields and one orange button

blocks.p: The booking card holds the whole search: From, To, Date, Class and Quota, then Search. From and To share a box, so the route reads as one thing. Class and Quota open with a value already in place.

figures.alt: The booking card with six numbered callouts covering the status tabs, the route box, the date, the class and quota menus, the six checkboxes and the Search button
figures.caption: Six things to notice on the card. Start at 6: Search is the only orange button on the whole page.

blocks.p: The card still carries six less common options as small checkboxes, such as the disability concession and flexible dates. I left them in view because some of them are access needs. The cost is a busier card. A way to tuck the rest away, without hiding those, would need testing.

People who already hold a ticket have a different job. For them, PNR Status (a PNR is the booking reference on a rail ticket) and Charts/Vacancy sit as two tabs on the card's top edge. Track Train is the first item in the menu.

figures.alt: The page header with six numbered callouts: helpline and email, text-size buttons, language menu, the four menu items, login and register, and the two emblems
figures.caption: The header in two rows. The grey bar holds help and the text-size buttons. The white row holds the menu and the login.

sections.label: Below the search
sections.heading: Everything else waits below the first screen

blocks.p: Under the search, ten other services appear as a grid of icons with short labels, from Flights and Hotels to Charter Train and Gallery. Icons keep this band light, like a menu.

figures.alt: Services band with the heading Find a suitable service for you here and ten navy icons in two rows of five
figures.caption: Ten shortcuts in two rows of five. All ten are the same size, so none of them competes with the search above.

blocks.p: Holidays come after that. Each of the five cards has a photo, an orange title, a paragraph and a Read more link. Someone booking a known route never has to read them.

figures.alt: Special Curated Holidays band with five navy cards in two rows, each with a photograph, an orange title and a paragraph
figures.caption: The five holiday cards. They start two screens down the page.

figures.alt: One holiday card enlarged, with a photograph of a train at night, an orange title and a long justified paragraph in white
figures.caption: One card up close. The paragraph is long, bold and justified, which makes it heavy to read. The cards are still the densest part of the page.

sections.label: Type and colour
sections.heading: Navy for structure, orange for one action

blocks.p: Navy carries almost everything: headings, icons, pills and the holiday cards. Orange is saved for the Search button and the card titles. The footer uses a darker indigo, so it reads as the end of the page.

figures.alt: Chart of eight text samples from 85 px to 15 px cut from the design, five colour swatches with their values, and three contrast measurements
figures.caption: Type samples cut from the design at full size, with the colours and three contrast measurements. Read the contrast column: two of the three fall short.

blocks.p: Measuring the mock-up shows two weaknesses. There are 13 text sizes between 12 and 85 px, more than a page like this needs. And the white Search label on orange has a contrast of 2.7 to 1, below the 3 to 1 that accessibility guidelines ask for large text. The grey 15 px option labels are low too, at 3.3 to 1.

figures.alt: End of the page: a social strip shading from orange to green with eight network icons, a dark indigo footer with 19 link groups, and a row of payment logos
figures.caption: The end of the page. A social strip in flag colours, then 19 link groups, each with an arrow to open it. The copyright line and payment logos are placeholder content.

sections.label: What comes next
sections.heading: What it would take to go further

blocks.p: This is one screen of a much longer journey. A calm homepage proves little until the screens after it handle the hard cases: no seats left, a changed fare, a route with no suitable train.

figures.alt: Diagram of a booking journey in five steps where only the first, the homepage and train search, is marked as designed, with four missing homepage states listed below
figures.caption: Where the concept stops. Only the first box was designed. The rest is drawn to show what a full booking redesign would have to cover.

list: Draw the homepage's own missing states: an empty or wrong field, the station list and the open date picker.
Design a phone-width version. The page exists at desktop width only.
Test three tasks with travellers: find a train, check an existing trip and find a concession option.
Raise the contrast of the Search label and the small grey text, and cut down the number of type sizes.

sections.label: What I learned
sections.heading: Order is the cheapest tool, and it is not enough

blocks.p: Putting the search first cost nothing and did most of the work. But position alone left gaps that only show up when you measure: headings lower down that are bigger than the main task, and an action colour that is hard to read.
The lesson I take from it is to settle the type scale and check contrast before drawing the first card.
